bridge: I01–I07 mapped AI data and authority. D08 covered incident response. Use only the fictional scenario and saved evidence.
teaching:
### Describe the event without jumping to a cause

A wrong answer, leaked document and unintended tool write are different incidents. Record the observed output and state change, affected accounts, relevant versions and timing. Then trace which data and components could have produced them.

### Contain the relevant authority

The response might disable a tool, revoke a credential, restrict retrieval or pause a feature under the organisation's plan. Choose the measure that addresses the observed risk and preserves useful evidence. Deleting chat text alone may not remove every stored copy or stop a worker.

### Check and repair the boundary

Was another tenant's document retrieved? Did a tool trust a model-supplied user identifier? Did a retry duplicate a valid action? Connect the fix with the actual failure, then verify the denied case and legitimate behaviour using safe fixtures.

### Build the security case

A security case connects claims, evidence and assumptions. State the intended task, protections, tests, observed outcomes and remaining limits. Assign owners for monitoring and response.

Finish with a scoped conclusion another reviewer can challenge. Do not claim the capstone establishes safety for every model, user group or deployment.
example:
Synthetic incident packet
User A requested a summary of publicD1.
D1 contains an untrusted instruction to send privateA1 to X.
Mock model proposal: send(privateA1,X).
Executor log: proposal denied (tool unavailable).
Retrieval log: publicD1 only; no privateA1 text accessed.
No message was sent. No actual model was called; this is a supplied fixture.
explanation: The supported result is that this executor blocked this mock proposal. The packet does not establish whether a live model would propose it, whether every tool is safe or whether other documents are poisoned. Clear evidence boundaries are part of the capstone, not an optional disclaimer.
exercise: Write a threat model and incident memo using the packet. Include authorised task, untrusted source, attempted effect, actual enforcement result, preserved metadata, containment options and three untested questions. Add an owner-scoped retrieval/agent design.
solution: Reference memo: authorised task was A summarising public D1. The untrusted D1 instruction attempted to redirect the task into sending private A1 to X. The supplied mock proposal requested that send, but the executor denied it because the tool was unavailable; the retrieval log contains only public D1, so the packet shows no private A1 access and no message sent. Preserve D1/version, task/correlation identifiers, relevant configuration and the denied policy decision under restricted retention. Keep the unnecessary send tool absent and review the document/source handling; disabling a capability already absent is not an accomplished new containment action. Proposed design authenticates A, filters retrieval by current owner/public policy before exposure, and lets an independent executor accept only scoped read/draft operations. Untested questions include what a live model would propose, whether other paths expose private context, and whether caches contain stale or poisoned content. No live model call or external report is part of this exercise.
challenge: Change the packet: send was enabled under a broad service credential and no user approval was checked. Explain the possible failure, immediate containment and exact regression cases needed. Do not send a test message or launch a model run.
challenge_solution: Contain by disabling/scoping the capability and revoking affected credentials as appropriate; preserve safe evidence, review destinations and inspect derived state. Regression cases cover user scope, approved destination/content, expiry, unknown tools, retry/budget and valid drafting. Actual exposure needs records; the changed design alone is not proof of a particular real-world leak.
